questions.question: What is DOM manipulation in JavaScript?
questions.title: DOM manipulation
questions.direct_answer: DOM manipulation is reading or changing the browser's in-memory document tree with APIs such as querySelector, createElement, setAttribute, and append. A DOM change can update content, attributes, classes, or structure; safe code keeps data separate from markup and changes only the required nodes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether DOM operations are understood as tree mutations.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming a selector always finds an element or using HTML parsing for plain text.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connecting node changes to safety and rendering cost.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: The DOM is the browser's object tree for a document.
querySelector finds the first element matching a CSS selector.
textContent writes text without parsing it as HTML.
createElement and append build structure without string concatenation.
Repeated layout reads and writes can cause avoidable rendering work.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The Document Object Model represents an HTML document as a tree of objects. JavaScript can select nodes, read their state, create new nodes, and change text, attributes, classes, or parent-child relationships.

For example, a todo form can create an `li`, set its `textContent` from the user's input, and append it to a list. The browser updates the rendered page because the underlying DOM tree changed.

Selection and mutation are separate steps. `document.querySelector` returns the first matching element or `null`, so code must handle a missing target. Methods such as `classList.toggle` express a class change more clearly than rebuilding an entire `className` string.

The main boundary is safety and cost. I use `textContent` for untrusted text because it is not parsed as markup, avoid rewriting a large container for one small change, and group related updates so the browser does not repeatedly recalculate layout. Frameworks automate parts of this process, but the same DOM rules still apply underneath.

sections.title: The rendered page follows an object tree
sections.content: HTML parsing creates document nodes. DOM APIs operate on those nodes, and the browser's rendering pipeline later turns their current structure and styles into pixels.

sections.title: Selection can fail and nodes have identity
sections.content:
A selector is evaluated against a document or element and may return no match. Once created, a node is one object: appending an existing node elsewhere moves it rather than making a copy. `cloneNode` creates a new node, but event listeners added with `addEventListener` are not copied.

DOM properties and HTML attributes are related but not always identical. For form controls, the current `input.value` property may differ from the original `value` attribute. Read the property when current live state is required.

sections.title: From HTML to a visible update
sections.content:
HTML text → parser → DOM tree
JavaScript selects a node → changes node state
style/layout → paint → pixels on screen

questions.question: What is the difference between textContent and innerHTML?
questions.title: textContent and innerHTML
questions.direct_answer: textContent reads or writes plain text for a node and its descendants, so characters such as angle brackets remain text. innerHTML serializes or parses HTML markup. Use textContent for ordinary or untrusted text; use innerHTML only when HTML parsing is genuinely required and the markup comes from a trusted or properly sanitized source.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether markup parsing is separated from plain-text insertion.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explaining both the security boundary and replacement of node identity.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: textContent treats its input as text, not markup.
innerHTML parses a string and replaces descendant nodes.
Untrusted innerHTML can create cross-site scripting vulnerabilities.
Replacing innerHTML discards the old descendant node objects.
Use DOM creation APIs when structured markup is assembled from data.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: `textContent` works with text. Assigning `"Ada"` displays those characters rather than creating a bold element, which makes it the normal choice for names, messages, labels, and other data. `innerHTML` works with serialized markup. Setting it invokes the HTML parser and replaces the element's descendants with newly parsed nodes. For example, a trusted template string containing `` can create a strong element, while the same string assigned to `textContent` remains visible text. The security boundary is important: interpolating user input into `innerHTML` can turn attacker-controlled markup or event-handler attributes into script execution. Escaping one character by hand is not a reliable sanitizer. Plain data belongs in `textContent`; rich untrusted HTML needs a reviewed sanitizer and policy. Replacing descendants also changes identity. References and listeners attached to old child nodes no longer describe the new tree. For data-driven structure I prefer `createElement`, property assignment, and `append`, because each value's role is explicit.

sections.title: One API writes data; the other asks for parsing
sections.content: The question is not which property is shorter. It is whether the input represents plain data or intentionally trusted HTML syntax.

sections.title: Parsing creates a new subtree
sections.content:
The `innerHTML` setter parses its string in the element's context. Table-related markup and namespace rules can affect the resulting nodes, so string concatenation is not equivalent to moving existing DOM nodes. Scripts inserted through `innerHTML` have special execution behaviour, but that does not make the API safe; many other injection paths remain.

`textContent` returns combined descendant text, including text that CSS may hide. `innerText` is layout-aware and closer to rendered text, so reading it can involve style calculation. Use the property whose meaning matches the task.

sections.title: Choose by input meaning
sections.content:
| API | Interprets value as | Main use | Main risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| `textContent` | Plain text | User/data values | Replaces child text |
| `innerHTML` | HTML markup | Trusted rich markup | Injection and replaced nodes |

sections.title: Keep data as text

questions.question: How can you reduce unnecessary DOM rendering work?
questions.title: Efficient DOM updates
questions.direct_answer: Reduce rendering work by changing only the necessary nodes, grouping related writes, and avoiding loops that alternate layout-dependent reads with writes. Build detached subtrees or a DocumentFragment before one insertion, and measure before optimizing because modern browsers already batch many operations.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether browser rendering cost is tied to concrete DOM access patterns.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling every DOM operation slow without measurement.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Recognising forced layout, batching, and the limits of micro-optimization.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Change the smallest DOM region that represents the new state.
Group writes instead of alternating layout reads and writes.
Use a DocumentFragment or detached element for a batch of new nodes.
Delegate repeated child events when it simplifies listener management.
Measure with browser performance tools before applying complex optimizations.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A DOM mutation can invalidate style or layout, but the expensive pattern is often forced synchronous layout: code writes a style, immediately reads a geometry property, then repeats that cycle for many elements.

For example, setting every card's width and then reading `offsetHeight` inside the same loop can make the browser repeatedly bring layout up to date. Reading all required measurements first and applying all writes afterward gives the engine more room to batch the work.

When inserting many nodes, I create them in a detached `DocumentFragment` and append the fragment once. The fragment itself disappears and its children move into the document. Updating one existing text node is still better than replacing a whole list when only one label changed.

The boundary is evidence. A fragment is not automatically faster for every small update, and browsers optimize common operations. I keep code simple, avoid obvious read-write thrashing, and use the Performance panel to find real style, layout, and paint costs before adding an elaborate caching layer.

sections.title: Rendering work follows invalidation and observation
sections.content: Writes mark parts of rendering state as dirty. A later geometry read may require the browser to calculate current layout immediately so it can return an accurate number.

sections.title: DOM layout reads and writes
sections.content:
Properties such as `offsetWidth`, `offsetHeight`, and `getBoundingClientRect()` may require up-to-date geometry. Reading them is normal; the issue is interleaving them with invalidating writes in a large loop. A read phase followed by a write phase breaks that repeated dependency.

For long collections, the biggest gain may be rendering fewer elements through pagination or virtualization. That changes application behaviour and accessibility, so it is a larger design decision than batching a small update.

sections.title: Avoid read-write thrashing
sections.content:
slow: write → forced layout read → write → forced layout read
better: read measurements → compute → write all changes
large insert: build detached nodes → append once

sections.title: Separate measurement from mutation
